text: June thirtieth, 1908. Siberia. In seconds, eighty million trees fall flat, and nobody can say what hit them.
Eighty million trees. Flattened like matchsticks. And there's no crater. No rock. No wreckage.
So what hit Earth that morning, and why did it leave nothing behind?
This is the Tunguska event, and a century later, scientists are still arguing about it.
Central Siberia was almost empty. Pine forest, swamp, and a few reindeer herders.
The Podkamennaya Tunguska River, thousands of kilometers from Moscow, and from anyone who could help.
At about seven-fifteen, a herder looked up and watched the sky turn white.
A fireball, brighter than the sun, streaked across the sky.
Then it vanished. And seconds later, the sky itself seemed to explode.
A shockwave tore through the forest, and tree after tree went down.
Sixty kilometers away, a trader said his shirt felt like it was on fire. The blast threw him off his porch.
Horses collapsed. Windows shattered. People felt the ground roll beneath their feet.
Scientists estimate the blast at around fifteen megatons, roughly a thousand Hiroshima bombs.
And it happened in the middle of nowhere, which is exactly why nobody went to look.
But the world noticed. Instruments in Britain recorded a pressure wave that circled the globe, twice.
For days, nights across Europe glowed. In London, people reportedly read newspapers at midnight.
People looked up and asked the same thing: what was that?
Nobody could answer. And nobody went to find out.
Russia was busy with wars and a revolution. For nineteen years, the site sat untouched.
Until 1927. A Russian mineral expert named Leonid Kulik was sure it was a giant meteorite.
He trekked for weeks through swamp and storm. His own guides were afraid to enter the zone.
He expected a crater as big as a stadium.
What he found was far stranger.
Millions of trees, lying flat, all pointing away from one spot, like a giant hand had swept them.
And at the center? Trees still standing, stripped of every branch, like telegraph poles.
No crater. Kulik drained swamps and dug for years. He never found the rock.
Something had wiped out an area bigger than London, without leaving a single fragment.
So what did this?
Theory one: a comet. Ice and dust would explode, then leave nothing behind.
Theory two: a lake. One team claimed a small lake nearby was the crater. Most scientists disagree.
Theory three: antimatter, or a tiny black hole. Exciting ideas, but nothing supports them.
Theory four: Nikola Tesla's death ray. The internet loves it. There is no evidence.
Theory five: aliens. That one started in 1946, with a science-fiction story about a spaceship exploding over Siberia.
Some readers took the story as fact. The legend never really died.
Dozens of theories. Decades of arguing. And still no clear answer.
Then in the sixties, researchers found something odd. Tiny melted spheres of glass and metal in the soil and tree resin.
Something had burned, and left only dust.
And those standing trees at the center told another story.
The blast hadn't come from the side. It came from straight above.
That pattern means one thing: an explosion in mid-air.
Most scientists now agree: a space rock about fifty meters wide slammed into the atmosphere at tens of thousands of kilometers an hour.
Under the pressure and heat, it couldn't survive. It exploded five to ten kilometers up.
An airburst. It explains everything: the flat trees, the standing trees, the missing crater.
The rock never hit Earth. It died in the sky, and the sky took the blow.
Case closed? Not quite.
Because in 2013, it almost happened again. A rock just twenty meters wide exploded over Chelyabinsk, Russia.
Windows shattered across a whole city. About fifteen hundred people were hurt, mostly by flying glass.
And that rock was far smaller than Tunguska's.
Scientists estimate rocks like Tunguska arrive every few hundred to a thousand years.
We were lucky in 1908. It hit a place with almost nobody living there.
Earth turns fifteen degrees every hour. Had it arrived a few hours later, it might have burst above a city.
An area bigger than London, flattened in seconds.
Today telescopes scan the sky for rocks like this. We've found most of the giant ones. The medium ones? Most are still undiscovered.
The next one is out there. We just don't know where.
